verses.text: Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;
And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour.
But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints;
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.
Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience.
Be not ye therefore partakers with them.
For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light:
(For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth;)
Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord.
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.
For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret.
But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light.
Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is.
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ;
Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God.
Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord.
For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body.
Therefore as the church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing.
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word,
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He that loveth his wife loveth himself.
For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church:
For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones.
For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.
This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.
Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband.

summary: The chapter opens with the most audacious imperative in the letter, stated as though it were obvious: "Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children." Imitation of God is made possible only by the family relation that precedes it, and its content is immediately narrowed to one thing — "walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour." The pattern to be imitated is a self-donation described in the vocabulary of the altar, so love here is defined by a death rather than by an emotion. What follows is the negative image of that love, and Paul sets three vices side by side that the ancient world would not have grouped together: "fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints." Sexual disorder and greed belong to the same family because both take rather than give. The regulation extends past conduct to speech — "Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient" — and the prescribed replacement is not solemnity but gratitude, "but rather giving of thanks," since thanksgiving is the speech of a person who has received rather than seized. Then a hard warning: "no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God," with covetousness explicitly named idolatry, and a caution against those who will soften it — "Let no man deceive you with vain words: for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience." Paul then reaches for the image that governs the middle of the chapter, and states it as identity rather than aspiration: "ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" — not in darkness and in light, but darkness and light. The command follows the fact: "walk as children of light," bearing "the fruit of the Spirit... in all goodness and righteousness and truth," and "Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord." The relation to surrounding corruption is neither participation nor silence: "have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them," a reproof that works by exposure, since "all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever doth make manifest is light." The section closes with what sounds like a fragment of an early baptismal hymn: "Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light." From there the tone becomes practical and urgent — "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" — with wisdom defined not as insight in general but as "understanding what the will of the Lord is." The contrast that follows is the chapter's structural pivot: "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit." Both are conditions in which a person is governed by something outside himself, and Paul specifies what Spirit-filling looks like in a series of participles that are all corporate and vocal: "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God." That last participle carries directly into the household instructions, so mutual submission is presented as the fourth mark of a Spirit-filled congregation rather than as a new subject. "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord" is grounded in a headship immediately qualified by rescue — "the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body." The husband's command is longer and costlier: "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it," and the purpose clauses describe not the husband's benefit but the beloved's transformation, "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish." Paul then argues from bodily self-interest — "He that loveth his wife loveth himself. For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church: For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones" — and quotes the founding text of marriage, "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh." The comment that follows is the most consequential sentence in the chapter: "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." Then, having ascended to the union of Christ and his body, Paul comes back down to the room: "Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband."
takeaways: Paul groups fornication, uncleanness and covetousness as a single category and then calls the third of them idolatry, which is a more radical claim than it appears. What binds them is acquisition: each treats another person or thing as material for one's own satisfaction, and each is therefore the exact inverse of the love just defined as Christ "hath given himself for us." The chapter's ethics of sex and its ethics of money are not two topics but one, and both are measured against a self-donation. Naming greed as idolatry also removes the comfortable distinction by which a respectable congregation deplores sexual sin while treating acquisitiveness as ambition, since the letter puts them under the same verdict about inheritance in the kingdom.

The command about speech is easy to misread as prudishness. "Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks" is not a prohibition on humour but on a particular use of speech — the corrosive, knowing, degrading wit that makes other people material for amusement — and the alternative offered is not silence or gravity but thanksgiving. That substitution is precise: the person whose habitual speech is gratitude has already conceded that he is a recipient, which is the disposition that makes both greed and contempt impossible. Read alongside the previous chapter's rule that speech should "minister grace unto the hearers," Paul is treating a community's ordinary conversation as one of its principal spiritual disciplines.

"Ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" states the change as a change of substance rather than of location or behaviour, and the imperative follows rather than produces it. This ordering is consistent across the letter and governs how the ethical chapters should be heard: the commands never construct an identity, they express one already conferred. The consequence for engagement with a corrupt world is equally carefully balanced — "have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them" — which is neither participation nor withdrawal but exposure. The mechanism is stated as almost passive: light does not argue, it makes things visible, so the first form of Christian reproof is the presence of a community whose ordinary life shows what the alternative actually costs.

"Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" sets two states of being governed against each other, and the comparison is more exact than it is flattering. Both involve a person acting under an influence he has admitted, and both alter speech and inhibition. The difference lies in what the influence produces: dissipation and loss of self on one side, and on the other four participles that are all outward-facing — singing to one another, praise directed to the Lord, thanksgiving "always for all things," and mutual submission. Notably Paul defines Spirit-filling almost entirely in terms of what a congregation does together, not by private experience, and includes yielding to other people as one of its constituent marks.

The household instructions begin under the heading of verse twenty-one, "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God," and the grammar of verse twenty-two depends on it, since the Greek supplies no second verb for the wives. That structure means the specific submissions that follow are instances of a mutuality that binds everyone, not exceptions to it, and it sets the frame in which the asymmetry of the commands must be read. The asymmetry is real and should not be smoothed away: wives are told to submit, husbands are not told to submit in the same words. But the husband's assignment is by far the heavier, since it is defined by the cross rather than by authority, and its stated aim is his wife's holiness rather than his own convenience — a headship measured entirely by what it gives up.

The sequence at the end moves in an unexpected direction. One would expect Paul to explain the union of Christ and the Church by appealing to marriage as an illustration; instead he treats the union of Christ and the Church as the reality and marriage as the thing that has been pointing to it since Eden. "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church" claims that the one-flesh clause of the creation account was always about more than a household. This inverts the usual order of explanation and gives ordinary marriage a weight it cannot carry on its own terms: it is a sign of something, and its obligations follow from what it signifies. The final verse then prevents the whole discussion from floating off into symbolism, returning to a particular man, a particular wife, and the daily work of love and reverence.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 2:24 — therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this verse and then says he is speaking of Christ and the Church, so the creation account is not decoration but the load-bearing text of his argument. In Genesis the one-flesh clause is the narrator's conclusion drawn from the woman being taken from the man's side, which explains Paul's otherwise odd phrase "members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones" — he is reading the Church as formed from Christ in the way Eve was formed from Adam. Reading the original also establishes that marriage was instituted before the fall and carries a meaning independent of it, which is why Paul can treat it as a sign rather than a concession.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 3:16-19 — let the word of Christ dwell in you richly... wives, submit yourselves; husbands, love your wives
crossRefs.why: The parallel passage runs the identical sequence — indwelling, psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, thanksgiving, then household instructions — but substitutes "let the word of Christ dwell in you richly" where Ephesians has "be filled with the Spirit," which is a useful check on both. It also states the husband's command with a warning attached, "and be not bitter against them," and gives the wife's submission a limiting qualifier, "as it is fit in the Lord." The compression in Colossians makes clear that Ephesians is expanding a shared pattern of instruction rather than inventing an argument for one congregation's local problem.

crossRefs.label: Hosea 2:19-20 — I will betroth thee unto me for ever... in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness
crossRefs.why: The prophetic tradition of God as husband to an unfaithful people is the background against which Paul's marriage analogy has to be heard. Hosea's God does not merely command fidelity but woos, purifies and betroths a bride who has already broken the covenant, which supplies the note of rescue in "he is the saviour of the body" and the purpose of cleansing in "that he might sanctify and cleanse it." The prophet also shows that the marriage image is not primarily about hierarchy but about covenant loyalty and the restoration of a ruined relationship, which shifts the centre of gravity in Ephesians 5 from authority to faithfulness.

crossRefs.label: Revelation 19:7-8 — the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready
crossRefs.why: Paul says Christ will "present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle," and the vision of the marriage supper supplies the scene toward which that presentation moves. The bride there is arrayed in fine linen explicitly identified as the righteousness of saints, which holds together the two things Ephesians asserts at once — that the cleansing is Christ's work and that the resulting holiness is genuinely the Church's own. Reading them together also makes clear that the chapter's marriage language is eschatological: the husband's love images something that has not yet reached its completion.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 60:1 — Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee
crossRefs.why: Verse fourteen's "Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light" is introduced with a formula of citation but matches no single scripture exactly, and this oracle is among the texts whose language it gathers — a summons to rise, a light arriving from outside, and a people who were in darkness. The prophetic setting, where the light on Zion draws the nations to her brightness, matches the movement of Ephesians from Gentile darkness to inclusion in the one body. It also explains why the summons is addressed to those already in covenant: the call to awake is not evangelistic recruitment but the rousing of a people who possess a light they are not yet walking in.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 2:3-8 — in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves... he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death
crossRefs.why: The letter to Philippi supplies the fullest statement of the logic underlying "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God" and the husband's command to love as Christ loved. There the mutual deference of a congregation is grounded in a descent from equality with God to the death of a slave, and the same descent is presented as the mind Christians are to have among themselves. Set beside Ephesians 5, it establishes that headship exercised as self-expenditure is not a softening of the concept but its Christian definition, and that mutual submission is a doctrine about Christ before it is a rule about households.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 6:9-10,16 — the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God... he which is joined to an harlot is one body
crossRefs.why: Corinth receives the same list of excluded conduct and the same conclusion about inheriting the kingdom, and it makes explicit what Ephesians assumes about why sexual sin is treated with such gravity. Paul there quotes the identical one-flesh clause from Genesis to argue that bodily union is never merely physical, and grounds the whole appeal in the body being a temple of the Holy Spirit. Read together, the passages show that the marriage theology of Ephesians 5 and the sexual ethics of its opening verses rest on one conviction, that union of bodies signifies and effects something real.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church," Catholic interpretation reads marriage as a sacrament in the proper sense: a sign instituted by Christ that not only represents the union of Christ and the Church but actually confers the grace it signifies. The word rendered "mystery" is the term that early Latin tradition translated as sacrament, and the passage is understood to mean that the one-flesh union established at creation was always ordered toward the union of Christ with his body, so that a Christian marriage participates in that union rather than merely illustrating it. From this follows the tradition's insistence on the indissolubility of a consummated sacramental marriage — since Christ does not abandon his Church, the sign cannot be dissolved without falsifying what it signifies — and its treatment of the spouses' mutual self-gift as a genuine means of sanctification. The purpose clauses of verses twenty-six and twenty-seven are also read as language of baptismal washing, so the chapter joins the sacrament that makes the Church to the sacrament that images her.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally hold that the word here means a previously hidden truth now revealed, as it plainly does earlier in this same letter, and that translating it as sacrament imports a later category the text does not carry. On this reading marriage is a creation ordinance and a divinely honoured estate rather than a sacrament, since the two rites the Reformers retained were those they judged to have been instituted by Christ with a promise of grace attached, and marriage predates the gospel and is shared with unbelievers. Most therefore read the analogy as profoundly instructive without conferring grace, and while regarding divorce as a grave evil, allow that Christ's own exception and the case of desertion admit dissolution in limited circumstances. Both traditions read the passage as making marriage far more than a contract, as grounding its obligations in Christ's own fidelity, and as forbidding the treatment of a spouse as a possession.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God" as the governing principle of the whole household section and reads the subsequent asymmetry within it rather than against it. Headship is understood as a real ordering within a communion of equal persons, not a difference of dignity, and it is defined by the model given — a head who "gave himself for it" and whose authority is exercised entirely as self-expenditure for the other's holiness. The tradition therefore reads the husband's command as by far the more demanding and reads the wife's submission as freely given within a mutual gift, while insisting that no reading which produces domination or reduces the wife to an instrument can be faithful to a text whose stated pattern is the cross. That the passage sits inside a discussion of Spirit-filling further indicates that these relations are meant to be lived as grace rather than enforced as law.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers divide sharply here. Complementarian interpreters argue that verse twenty-one describes submission within appropriate relations rather than an undifferentiated mutuality, and that a distinct male headship in the home is taught by the analogy itself, since the Church does not exercise headship over Christ. Egalitarian interpreters press the grammar of verse twenty-two, which borrows its verb from verse twenty-one, and read the household instructions as a subversion of the ancient household codes from within — each subordinate party is addressed as a moral agent and each dominant party is given the harder command. Both Protestant camps agree with the Catholic reading that the husband's love is defined by Christ's self-giving, that headship in this passage never authorises coercion, and that the wife is addressed as a person capable of her own free obedience to the Lord.

interpretationNotes.claim: The clause "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word" is read in Catholic tradition as a direct reference to baptism, and as evidence that the sacrament genuinely effects what it signifies. The washing is not said to picture cleansing but to accomplish it, the agent is Christ, and the instrument is water joined to the word — a formula the tradition reads as the pattern of sacramental action generally, in which a material sign and the word of Christ together convey grace. Because the object cleansed is the Church rather than an individual, the verse also grounds the conviction that baptism incorporates a person into a body rather than merely settling a private transaction, which is why the letter can move from washing to the presentation of a whole glorious Church without spot or wrinkle.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that baptism is in view but locate the effective agent in the word rather than the water, noting that Paul specifies "by the word" and reading the washing as the sign and seal of a cleansing accomplished by Christ's blood and received by faith. Reformed and Lutheran readers differ among themselves about how closely the sign and the thing signified are joined, with Lutherans holding a genuinely instrumental view close to the Catholic one; Baptist readers stress that the washing follows faith and signifies a cleansing already granted. Many also emphasise that the whole sentence is about Christ's action on the Church and warn against any reading that transfers the efficacy to the minister or the rite considered by itself. Both traditions confess that the cleansing is Christ's work, that it is corporate as well as personal, and that it is aimed at a holiness to be completed at his presentation of the Church to himself.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
